v.why: With fan-in-scaled init and Adam's roughly fixed per-parameter step, wide nets change their function more per step and so hit the LR instability cliff at smaller LR.
At large LR, bigger batches reduce gradient noise and the number of risky large updates, stabilizing training.
At tiny LR the fixed 243-epoch budget makes update count the bottleneck, so fewer steps from larger batches causes underfitting.
The L2 term is scaled by 1/batch_size in sklearn-style MLPs, so larger batches relieve over-shrinkage precisely when alpha is large.
Composing more layers amplifies large Adam updates into instability, so adding depth hurts most at high LR.
Large batches give few, low-noise updates per epoch, so a larger LR is both tolerated and needed to converge in budget.
Three-layer stacks reach the LR instability cliff earlier than one-layer nets, so raising LR is more harmful for them.
With per-batch penalty scaling of alpha/batch_size, small batches amplify the effective L2 strength, so raising alpha over-regularizes sooner.
Wider nets make more function-space progress per small Adam step, partially compensating for an undersized learning rate.
Deeper nets need more updates to optimize, so adding layers hurts most when large batches leave few steps in the 243-epoch budget.

raw:
Seven hypotheses condition on the edited parameter's own value, so I discarded them: the four learning-rate/learning-rate ones, the two alpha/alpha ones, and batch_size up given batch_size high.

Thirteen remained, covering nine distinct (edit, condition) pairs. Where several shared a pair, I kept one per pair:
- **learning_rate_init × width:** kept "width high". It is the less obvious direction.
- **learning_rate_init × batch_size:** kept "batch_size high". It is the more contestable one.
- **batch_size × learning_rate_init:** kept both "LR high" (gradient-noise stability) and "LR low" (update-count budget). Their mechanisms differ, and this fills the tenth slot. I dropped "batch_size down given LR low" because it repeats the update-count mechanism.
